content: 1. The point estimates exhibit overlapping confidence intervals, with an I² value of 59%. This level of heterogeneity cannot be attributed to small subgroup sizes and may indicate moderate heterogeneity. 2. Imprecision was downgraded once due to the small sample sizes of the studies, which ranged from 24 to 125 participants per group. The confidence interval does not cross the null value. 3. Inconsistency was downgraded twice. The point estimates are aligned in the same direction, with no overlap in confidence intervals, and an I² value of 89%. This substantial heterogeneity cannot be explained by small subgroup sizes. 4. Inconsistency was downgraded once. Most point estimates are similar, with overlapping confidence intervals, and an I² value of 78%. This substantial heterogeneity cannot be explained by small subgroup sizes. 5. Inconsistency was downgraded once. Some point estimates are similar, with some overlap in confidence intervals, and an I² value of 83%. This substantial heterogeneity cannot be explained by small subgroup sizes. 6. Inconsistency was not downgraded for an I² value of 34%. 7. Inconsistency was downgraded once. The point estimates differ without overlapping confidence intervals but are aligned in the same direction, with an I² value of 93%. This considerable heterogeneity cannot be explained by small subgroup sizes. 8. An additional report from the same trial (Shojaei 2017, Ref. ID 22030) assessed self-efficacy at six months using the Behavior Questionnaire. The estimate reported here was obtained using the Multidisciplinary Work-related LBP Predictor Questionnaire (self-efficacy subscale), which was also used to assess self-efficacy in the immediate term (closest to two weeks) (Shojaei 2017, Ref. ID 25009). 9. High statistical heterogeneity (I² = 81%) was observed, which could not be explained by small subgroup sizes. As a result, the evidence was downgraded twice. 10. Trials on health-related quality of life stratified by gender, race/ethnicity, or in adults from lowor lower-middle-income countries were not identified. Similarly, no trials on psychological functioning, social participation, changes in medication use, health literacy, or adverse events/harms were identified. 11. For older adults (aged 60 years or more), the certainty of evidence was assessed based on the number of patients, effect size, and study design. The risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and other considerations were evaluated. 12. Risk of bias was downgraded twice when trials were rated as having an overall high or unclear risk of bias. 13. Inconsistency was downgraded once when point estimates were similar with overlapping confidence intervals (I² = 60%), but the heterogeneity could not be explained by small subgroup sizes, indicating moderate heterogeneity. 14. Indirectness was not downgraded when trials were conducted in different countries (highor upper-middle-income settings). 15. Imprecision was downgraded twice due to small sample sizes, as the optimal information size (OIS) was not reached. The confidence interval crosses the null value. 16. Inconsistency was not downgraded when no additional studies were available for comparison. 17. Indirectness was downgraded once when evidence was derived from a single trial conducted in a single center in a high-income country. 18. Imprecision was downgraded twice due to small sample sizes, as the OIS was not reached. 19. Structured exercise therapies or programs are defined as planned, structured, repetitive, and purposeful physical activities aimed at improving or maintaining physical fitness components. These interventions are prescribed or planned by health workers and may be standardized or individualized. 20. Participants emphasized the importance of continuity in physical exercises to maintain mobility and reduce pain. A lack of continuity and instruction could lead to adverse effects, such as injuries. 21. Participants expressed a preference for educational materials with drawings and descriptions of exercises to support physical interventions.
